https://baltic-review.com/tallinn-digita.text: Share Tweet 0 Tallinn will host international programmes focused on digital innovation and entrepreneurship in August 2026. Two international education programmes beginning in Tallinn on 10 August will place Estonia’s digital society and startup environment at the centre of practical learning for students and early-stage entrepreneurs. TalTech’s Digital Innovation Summer School will run from 10 to 21 August, while the Estonian Business School’s sixth International Summer School on Digitalisation and Sustainability is scheduled for 10–14 August. A separate Young Entrepreneurs Summer School, organised by Estonian Business School and Startup Wise Guys, will take place in Tallinn from 10 to 16 August. The programmes are not commercial conferences or large public festivals. Instead, they are designed around workshops, group projects, mentoring and direct contact with Estonia’s technology and business communities. Their arrival offers a compact illustration of how Tallinn’s universities and innovation organisations are using the city as a working laboratory for digital development. From digital policy to practical solutions TalTech’s programme is structured around real-world digital governance challenges. According to the university’s published programme, participants will work in international teams on solutions connected with digital identity, interoperability, artificial intelligence ethics and digital society development. The format combines lectures and seminars with practical group work. Participants are expected to define a challenge, develop a prototype and present a solution blueprint at the end of the two-week course. The schedule also includes a visit to a technology hub or university laboratory, giving the teams an opportunity to connect policy questions with research and emerging technologies. This approach reflects a wider shift in technology education. Rather than treating digitalisation as a purely technical subject, the programme links software and data systems with public administration, organisational change and responsible implementation. For Estonia, whose public services are widely associated with digital access and interoperability, the country provides a particularly relevant setting for this kind of applied study. Entrepreneurship built around doing The Estonian Business School’s programmes take a more business-oriented route. Its International Summer School on Digitalisation and Sustainability is intended to examine the connection between entrepreneurship, technology and sustainable development. The Young Entrepreneurs Summer School, meanwhile, is a seven-day programme for ambitious young people from Estonia and abroad. The organisers describe a schedule that includes hands-on workshops, visits to Estonian startups, mentorship from founders and investors, a hackathon and a final demonstration day. Participants are expected to work on identifying problems, speaking with potential customers, developing solutions and presenting ideas. The programme also places emphasis on international connections. Its organisers say previous participants have come from more than ten countries, while the 2026 edition is open to young entrepreneurs from different academic and professional backgrounds. Need-based scholarships are available, according to the programme’s information page. For students, the value of such programmes is practical exposure to the early stages of company-building. For Estonia, they provide an opportunity to present its universities, startup companies and digital institutions to a temporary international audience without requiring participants to commit to a long-term study programme. A small-scale test of Estonia’s innovation model The three programmes differ in emphasis, but they share a common structure: international participants, technology-related problem-solving and direct interaction with companies or research organisations. This makes the week beginning 10 August more than a collection of separate summer courses. It also highlights the relationship between Estonia’s education sector and its broader economic strategy. Innovation ecosystems depend not only on research funding or successful companies, but also on the ability to attract people, share expertise and turn ideas into prototypes or viable products. Short, intensive programmes can contribute to that process by bringing together students, mentors, researchers and founders in the same environment. The immediate economic effect of the courses is likely to be modest. Their longer-term value lies in relationships and skills: potential co-founders meeting one another, students learning how Estonian organisations approach digital transformation, and local institutions gaining international visibility. As Tallinn prepares for the start of the programmes, the city will again serve as a meeting point for two strands of Estonia’s innovation identity: the public-sector experience of building digital services and the private-sector ambition to create globally scalable businesses. The result will be a constructive, hands-on snapshot of how technology education and entrepreneurship are being connected in Estonia. https://www.azernews.az/region/262699.ht.text: Latvia detains 28 migrants who entered from Belarus through border tunnel 22 August 2026 09:00 (UTC+04:00) Latvian border guards have detained 28 migrants who crossed the country’s eastern border from Belarus through an underground tunnel, according to Latvian authorities. The tunnel, discovered approximately 20 metres from the border, had been concealed under moss. It is the second such passage uncovered by Latvian authorities in recent weeks. On August 10, border guards discovered another tunnel that had reportedly been used by 15 migrants to enter Latvia from Belarus. Latvia has recorded a sharp increase in attempts at irregular border crossings in recent months. European leaders have described the growing migration pressure along the EU’s eastern borders as part of what they regard as a hybrid operation linked to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s government. The developments come as Latvia prepares for parliamentary elections scheduled for October 3. The country, with a population of around 2 million, has already recorded nearly 10,000 attempts to cross its border illegally during the first eight months of 2026. This compares with approximately 12,000 attempts recorded during the whole of 2025. Latvian authorities have reported that on some days more than 100 attempts are made to cross the 173-kilometre border, which is protected by a fence. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/16/at-l.text: At least 60 small-scale miners are dead, with many missing, after the collapse of a gold mine in Sudan's West Kordofan region.The mine reportedly began to collapse on Tuesday after two shafts that had been dug close together began to give way.Survivors say they do not know how many people remain trapped.One surviving miner Khair al-Sayyed Jabara told AFP there had been an overnight rescue operation since the collapse, and that fellow miners were having to dig using the same rudimentary tools they use to mine."Everyone's working very hard to retrieve the bodies or any survivors, but it's difficult. We need heavy machinery to clear the rock and soil."Heavy machinery is often not readily available at small-scale mining sites. Sudan’s gold industry has become increasingly important since the civil war began in April 2023, providing a significant source of revenue in an economy devastated by conflict.The civil war began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. As a result, the country is facing the world’s largest displacement crisis, with nearly 20 million people experiencing crisis-level hunger.

https://www.dw.com/en/will-germany-have-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MzF7 Compared to previous years, natural gas storage levels in Germany are low Image: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement As of mid-September 2026, Germany had stored just about 141 terawatt-hours of gas, accounting for around 57% of the country's total storage capacity. Last winter just under 134 terawatt-hours of gas were withdrawn from storage, according to the Federal Network Agency, the agency that monitors the country's electricity and gas networks. At first glance, the numbers sounds reassuring, especially since last winter was quite cold and therefore required a lot of heating. But compared to previous years, natural gas storage levels are low . On September 4, Markus Söder , the premier of Bavaria, called for intervention by the federal government. Rising fuel prices put pressure on German drivers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video A few days later, the opposition Green Party accused the economy minister of negligence. "The gas storage facilities are not full. We are facing a potential shortage," said Britta Hasselmann, co-leader of the Greens' parliamentary group. Such statements have raised concerns about potential gas shortages in Germany this winter. To assess the current situation, however, various factors such as imports and the diversification of supply sources need to be taken into account , not least since Germany is no longer as dependent on a single importer as it was on Russia until 2022. Will Germany have enough gas? Most experts interviewed by DW are not concerned about the winter gas supply. Charlie Grüneberg, spokesperson for the German Gas and Hydrogen Industry association, points to the contracts that have been signed for the medium term. "Anyone who has contractually secured their gas needs for the winter with a reliable supplier will receive the agreed quantities," he said. Sebastian Heinermann, managing director of INES, a German association for gas and hydrogen storage system operators, is more cautious. He pointed out that it's technically possible to fill gas storage facilities in Germany to around 77%, but this would require filling at a level that "has not been observed even once in the past three weeks," Heinermann said. "If this trend continues unchanged, the fill level will reach only about 65% by November 1." Most natural gas is stored underground at facilities like these in Jemgum on the Lower Ems Image: Astora Still, the Federal Network Agency sees no cause for concern. "The gas supply in Germany is stable," the agency's spokesperson, Nadia Affani, told DW. "Security of supply is currently guaranteed. Based on the latest information, the Federal Network Agency continues to assess the risk of a gas supply crunch as low." Germany's Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy shared a similar assessment. The ministry "is monitoring all developments very closely to ensure security of supply. There are currently no signs of a supply shortage," said spokesperson Susanne Ungrad. Officials downplay supply risks She also pointed to an array of factors that determine the price of natural gas like available storage, ongoing imports via pipelines and LNG terminals, demand and the situation on the international energy markets. "We are prepared for further developments," Ungrad stressed. Grüneberg also takes a more holistic view. "The key factor is whether enough gas can be procured and transported to and through Germany. Supply contracts, storage facilities, pipeline imports and LNG are all interlinked," he underscored. "Thanks to investments in LNG terminals, new import routes and reverse-flow capabilities, the infrastructure is now significantly more robust than it was in 2022." Gas prices rise ahead of winter As the winter approaches and people start heating their homes more, gas prices tend to climb. This trend is already evident, said Heinermann. "In the second quarter, the gas price across various contracts on the futures market stood at around €46 ($52) per megawatt-hour. Recently, the gas price has risen to over €80." Olaf Geyer from the US consulting firm Arthur D. Little, who has been monitoring the German market, said there is no immediate supply problem, but: "If the winter turns out to be cold or there are disruptions on the import side, prices could rise quickly." Grüneberg said "reliable price forecasts" are difficult to make and noted that low storage levels could cause prices to rise "if additional volumes have to be procured on the market." However, there are no signs of a shortage on the supply side. "As things stand today, there are no indications of a physical shortage of supply by the end of winter. The futures markets are not signaling this at the moment either," said Grüneberg. Can Germany refit gas pipelines to transport cleaner energy? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The German economy ministry points out that "the prices currently quoted for forward contracts for the winter are only slightly higher than the spot market prices for immediate transactions." "The usual summer-winter spread, which made it economically viable to store gas during the summer months, was therefore not present," it added. The "spread" is based on the principle of buying gas cheaply in summer and selling it at higher prices in winter. This year, gas prices rose following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz , undermining that seasonal pattern. How to refill storage faster Geyer, who also focuses on the summer-winter spread, said storage facilities aren't fuller this time round because it hasn't been economically viable. "For the future, we need better incentives for filling storage facilities — and risk management on the part of utilities that looks not only at the purchase price but also at how much actual consumption can deviate from projections," he underlined. Heinermann also called for effective economic incentives to fill gas storage facilities. "In the medium term, Germany needs a reliable market framework that, through incentives, obligations or a combination of both, ensures sufficient storage levels on a long-term basis while preserving as much market-based flexibility as possible." Fine Arts Behold the Beauty: ‘Jews Praying in the Synagogue on Yom Kippur’ Jews commemorate the ‘Day of Atonement,’ when Moses came down the mountain after seeking God’s forgiveness. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print A detail of “Jews Praying in the Synagogue on Yom Kippur,” 1878, by Maurycy Gottlieb. Oil on canvas; 96 inches by 75 inches. Tel Avivi Museum of Art, Tel Aviv. Public Domain Lorraine Ferrier 9/19/2026 | Updated: 9/19/2026 0:00 X 1 As the sun sets on Sept. 20, 2026, Jews begin Yom Kippur, the “Day of Atonement.” For Jews, this holy day marks when Moses descended Mount Sinai after receiving Yahweh’s forgiveness for the people of Israel, after they committed idolatry. Jews commemorate Yom Kippur through ascetic practices, such as fasting, and by attending five prayer services held in the synagogue throughout the day. According to the late rabbi, author, and philosopher Jonathan Sacks (1948–2020), “The question God asks [Jews] on Yom Kippur is not, ‘Are you perfect?’ but ‘Can you grow?’” A Personal Homage to Faith One can imagine that Polish painter Maurycy Gottlieb (1856–1879) meditated on such questions while painting “Jews Praying in the Synagogue on Yom Kippur,” especially because he depicted himself three times. In the lower left, he’s the young boy dressed in ornate golden brocade attire, wearing a pendant, and resting his hand on an open prayer book. He stands next to a pile of sacred manuscripts and the “shofar,” a ceremonial horn (usually a ram’s horn) blown to announce the end of Yom Kippur. On the far right, he’s an older boy dressed in black, studying with an elder, indicating his diligent sacred study. He might be approaching the time of his “Bar Mitzvah.” To the right of the “bimah,” the lectern where the Torah rests, Gottlieb is an adult deep in contemplation. He leans one arm on the bimah and holds his head, and the other hand keeps his place in a prayer book. He’s wearing a colorful “tallit,” the tasseled prayer shawl, and the same pendant he wore as a boy, hinting at the faith he’s held since boyhood. “Jews Praying in the Synagogue on Yom Kippur,” 1878, by Maurycy Gottlieb. Oil on canvas; 96 inches by 75 inches. Tel Aviv Museum of Art, Tel Aviv. Public Domain In addition to his own presence, Gottlieb also surrounded himself with people from his youth in Drohobycz, in the Commonwealth of Poland (modern-day Ukraine). His sweetheart, Laura Rosenfeld, appears twice, standing in the gallery reserved for women. On the left, she’s poised, holding a prayer book, and, on the right, Gottlieb rendered her standing and supporting her mother. In the center, the rabbi holds the cylindrical Torah scroll close. While most of the male figures wear a “kippah,” a cap that covers the crown, the rabbi wears a “streimel,” a traditional hat with a wide brim of fox, minx, or marten fur, which is reserved for special occasions. Related Stories Old Masters Reclaimed: Art Stolen by Nazis on Display at Jewish Museum Cherishing Judaica: Jewish Objects Around Boston Gottlieb inscribed his own epitaph on the Torah scroll mantle: “Donated in memory of our late honored teacher and rabbi Moshe Gottlieb of blessed memory 1878.” (Moshe was the artist’s forename in Hebrew). He died unexpectedly a few months later, some say of a heartbreak from his sweetheart marrying another. Cherishing Jewish Life Gottlieb reverently rendered life in the synagogue and the solemnity of Yom Kippur in this painting. Polish artist Leopold Pilichowsky (1869–1933) wrote: “Gottlieb was the first Jewish artist who perceived the poetry and beauty of Jewish life in exile. He was the first who saw in the lives of the poorly dressed Polish Jews, in their women and children, a highly developed rhythm, beauty, character, and type of culture. He understood, with his artistic knowledge and instinct, that the tallit can be used by the artist to create lines no less beautiful than the Greek or Roman toga.” Gottlieb’s “Jews Praying in the Synagogue on Yom Kippur” is also all the more poignant as the artist died young, at 23. It therefore acts as a stark reminder of the importance of self-reflection and repentance, as this transient life can take an unexpected turn through God’s grace. Authorities say one suspect photographed Ādaži Military Base by private aircraft. Searches uncovered electronic devices and documents as the investigation into potential espionage and sabotage support continues. by TVP World | Oct. 2, 2026, 10:54 am Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied One of the suspects allegedly took aerial photographs of the facility using a small private aircraft. Photo: vdd.gov.lv Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Latvia has detained two of its citizens on suspicion of collecting and passing information on the country’s defense sector to Russian intelligence, Latvian authorities have said. The Latvian State Security Service (VDD) said the two suspects gave Russian Military Intelligence (GRU) information about Latvia’s defense systems, the activities of NATO allies and on the forms of support for Ukraine. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . The case comes amid heightened concern across NATO’s eastern flank over Russian sabotage and other hybrid operations targeting countries supporting Ukraine. The couple was detained on June 28 in cooperation with the Latvia’s Defense Intelligence and Security Service (MIDD). Criminal proceedings have been opened against them on suspicion of collecting and transferring non-disclosable material and other information to a foreign intelligence service. Advertisement According to the VDD, the suspects also gathered information about a Latvian National Armed Forces aviation base, radar systems and the movements of military aircraft. One of the suspects allegedly carried out reconnaissance of the Ādaži Military Base, one of Latvia’s key military facilities and home to NATO’s multinational brigade in the country. The suspect apparently took aerial photographs of the facility using a small private aircraft on behalf of the GRU. Other Topics of Interest Russian Attack Kills 1 in Kyiv High-Rise, Shuts Down Bridges Across the Capital Kyiv closed three major bridges after overnight strikes as air defenses intercepted or suppressed 88 of 108 Russian drones, officials said. Authorities also allege that the pair carried out activities that could support potential Russian intelligence and sabotage groups operating in Latvia. On the day of the arrests, the VDD and MIDD searched three locations in Riga and Ādaži municipality in central Latvia. They seized electronic data storage devices, documents, and notes, which are being examined as part of the investigation. “The suspects have been taken into custody as a security measure,” the VDD said in a statement. https://www.politico.eu/article/icc-wins.text: STRASBOURG — The International Criminal Court has won this year's Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought, awarded by the European Parliament, according to two people with knowledge of the decision. The €50,000 prize honors defenders of human rights and freedom of thought, with past winners including Nelson Mandela, Alexei Navalny, Belarusian journalists, and the people of Ukraine. The Socialists and Democrats group nominated the ICC following U.S. President Donald Trump's sanctions on the court, announced on Oct. 9. "We stand by the ICC and its officials, and we are committed to safeguarding its work. We must guarantee that the ICC is able to operate independently, free from pressure or external interference," said S&D vice-chair Yannis Maniatis in early October. "It is a people-based organization, not a political one. If the aggressors become the victims, and if we stand by helplessly as international justice erodes, we risk allowing those who believe themselves above the law to prevail." The prize is named in honor of Andrei Sakharov, a Soviet physicist and political dissident. Shortlisted candidates are traditionally invited to the Parliament’s award ceremony, which takes place during the December plenary session in Strasbourg. Advertisement Advertisement
